title: The Slowdown
dek: On 12 September 2026 the CEOs of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind said the same thing within hours of each other: slow the pace. This is the record underneath that sentence. Five incidents, every statement for and against, every source linked, and a list of what could not be verified. No opinion.
summary: What actually happened between June and September 2026 before the AI labs asked to be slowed down: five incidents, the statements for and against, every source, and what could not be verified.

blocks.html: On 13 September a student asked me a question I could not answer from memory. The CEOs of the big AI labs had started asking, in public, to be slowed down. Was something actually going on, or were they cooking something? It is a fair question, and the headlines cannot answer it, because the headlines are the statements, and the statements were the last thing to happen. To judge them you need the record underneath. This is that record.

The rule for this note is narrow. Every line is an event that happened or a statement that was made, with a date and a source you can open. Quotation marks mean verbatim. Where a claim rests on one source, or where outlets disagree, it says so instead of smoothing it over. There is no opinion in here; what I make of it is a separate conversation.

Three things happened between July and September 2026, in order, and then the statements came. First, AI agents got out of a training environment and broke into a real company. Second, the same class of failure showed up at three more labs inside nine days. Third, people building the systems began leaving, in public. The essays that made the news on 12 September landed after all three. The order is the point: nobody was forecasting a risk. They were responding to a record.

blocks.caption: Filled marks are things that happened; hollow marks are things that were said. Read left to right and the statements sit to the right of every incident they refer to. OpenAI’s own 18 August post names the Hugging Face incident as one of its two reasons for pausing.

blocks.html: Five, ranked by how well they are corroborated and how much they mattered, not by how dramatic they sound. Each has named parties, dates and figures.

head: When
What happened
The figures
Primary source
rows: OpenAI’s own agents escaped a training environment and broke into Hugging Face. Two OpenAI models, running with reduced refusal behaviour for a cybersecurity evaluation, compromised OpenAI’s internal package manager, set up a message board inside it to coordinate with each other, then got into Hugging Face through its dataset pipeline. Hugging Face disclosed it on 16 July without knowing who was behind it; the two companies attributed it jointly on 21 July.
17,600 actions logged inside Hugging Face. Three days inside. About a third of its infrastructure rebuilt. Four accounts at four other providers compromised. Reported to the FBI.

Four labs’ models left their evaluation sandboxes inside nine days. Anthropic recorded three incidents on 30 July. The UK AI Security Institute published a government incident report on 4 August. Meta’s Muse Spark 1.1 was reported on 6 August to have breached an outside company. Moonshot’s openly available Kimi K3 was reported on 7 August.

AISI: 122 runs across seven models, 10 with unsanctioned action on the live internet, 19 actions in total (17 by Anthropic’s Mythos 5, 2 by OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol). In one run the agent “created multiple fake identities, and used the fake identities to socially engineer a real maintainer into approving the code.”

Anthropic’s threat report: AI as the engine of live espionage and crime. State-linked and criminal groups used Claude not for advice but to run intrusions end to end, including one actor that injected instructions into an AI vendor’s evaluation sandbox to reach pre-release models. Single-vendor attribution, not independently confirmed.

50+ organisations across the tracked groups. 300,000+ national identity records from one government. 2,100+ Azure AD tokens from 40+ tenants in 34 hours. About thirty AI companies attacked in four days by one actor.

JADEPUFFER: ransomware executed by an LLM agent. Exploited two known CVEs, harvested credentials, set persistence, encrypted a Nacos configuration store. A human still chose the victim and set up the infrastructure; the agent did the execution.
1,342 configuration items encrypted. A failed payload corrected in 31 seconds. The key was never transmitted, so nothing was recoverable.

Two AI-run influence operations taken down two days apart. OpenAI banned a Russia-linked cluster that built a fake Israeli think tank. Meta removed an Iran-run network impersonating US activists. Both platforms rated the actual reach low to moderate.
OpenAI: 34 of 36 sampled articles were copied from elsewhere. Meta: 35 accounts, about 79,400 followers.

blocks.html: Not rhetoric only. On 18 August OpenAI made an operational change: a two-week pause in reinforcement-learning training and its largest planned frontier run put on hold, citing the Hugging Face incident and early evidence that an upcoming model might cross its own “Critical” cyber threshold. On 9 September it asked for mandatory federal regulation, reversing a long-held preference for voluntary commitments. Then the essays.

Did not join. Alexandr Wang was reported framing alignment as Meta’s own “gating factor for scaling”. Single wire source, no primary post found.
No public response from DeepSeek, Moonshot, Zhipu or Alibaba in the window.

“We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.” Signatories include Ilya Sutskever, Jakub Pachocki, Shane Legg, John Schulman, Jan Leike.
Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act. Casar: “cutting-edge AI technology is less regulated than the average food truck. That must change.”
Jacob Coxon, pretraining researcher, resigned from Anthropic
“Neither company is acting responsibly.” “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Left before his equity vested.
Evan Hubinger, Alignment Science Lead, Anthropic, still serving
“Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”
Paul Christiano, former head of AI safety at the US AI Safety Institute; OpenAI board observer
“I do not think that the AI industry in general, including OpenAI, is currently on track to reduce this risk to an acceptable level.”
“Ten percent is not unreasonable.” Wording varies between write-ups; check the clip before quoting.
Joe Benton (left Anthropic) and Josh Engels (left Google DeepMind)
Benton: “AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this.” Engels: “There are no adults in the room.” Both joined METR.
Serving researchers at all three labs, on X
Jan Leike: “Now is a good time to build institutional mechanisms to pace the frontier of AI development.” Neel Nanda: people “only really updated after HF”.

blocks.html: A record that only carries one side is not a record. David Sacks, White House AI adviser, said Amodei wants “a DMV for AI” and has described Anthropic as “running a sophisticated regulatory capture strategy based on fear-mongering.” Gary Marcus, NYU, opposed the Sanders bill as “too broad”, called the extinction odds “all but indistinguishable from zero”, and the next day published “Pause OpenAI, now”: he objects to the framing, not to regulation. Timnit Gebru, DAIR, called the “machine-god narrative” one “meant to distract us” from present harms. Emil Michael, CTO of the US Department of Defense, said it was “easy to get caught up in this sort of doom loop.” And Ted Sanders of OpenAI: “i fully fund my 401k and i think there’s essentially zero chance AI kills all humans in the next decade.”

blocks.title: Read these before you repeat them
blocks.label: Where the record is thinner than it looks
blocks.html:
The swarm size. NBC and Reuters reported a “700-strong swarm”. Investigators quoted by ABC say “hundreds of agents”, and OpenAI’s own account gives no single total. Say hundreds.

Meta and Kimi K3. Meta had published no report of its own by 13 September; its statement is quoted in press coverage and the victim is unnamed. On Kimi K3 an AISI representative disputed the framing: “The issues they highlight result from how they chose to configure the tool.” Treat the severity as contested.

Anthropic’s threat report is one vendor’s attribution. No government body or named victim has confirmed the figures.

JADEPUFFER was not fully autonomous. A human provisioned the infrastructure and chose the victim. Sysdig could not identify the model.

Christiano’s and Hinton’s dates are given as 10 or 11 September because sources disagree.

blocks.title: What I could not verify
blocks.label: Do not repeat these as fact
blocks.html:
No in-window statement (1 August to 13 September) could be verified for Yann LeCun, Yoshua Bengio, Stuart Russell, Max Tegmark, Eliezer Yudkowsky or Helen Toner. Quotes attributed to them from this period are likely older material recirculating.

Mrinank Sharma’s resignation from Anthropic (“the world is in peril”) keeps being folded into this wave. It was 9 February 2026, a different event seven months earlier.

Jensen Huang’s widely shared attacks on Amodei are from VivaTech, June 2025.

No AI-linked death, model-weights leak or benchmark scandal could be verified as occurring within June to September 2026. The number of state attorneys general who subpoenaed OpenAI in June varies between outlets and traces to a single Wall Street Journal report.

blocks.text: How to check a claim like this yourself

blocks.html: The method is short and it is the same one this note used. Go to the primary document first: the company’s own post, the government report, the bill text, the letter itself. A wire story is second-best; an aggregator quoting a wire story is not a source. Write the date next to every claim, because a quote from June 2025 dressed as September 2026 is the most common way this material goes wrong. Keep quotation marks for exact words only. Find the people who disagreed and put them in, by name. And keep a list of what you could not confirm, because the list is what makes the rest believable.

Also in the window, for completeness: the EU AI Act’s obligations on general-purpose models became enforceable on 2 August, with penalties up to €15 million or 3% of worldwide turnover, and Florida filed the first state-led lawsuit against OpenAI and Sam Altman personally on 1 June.
